Summary  
This paper introduces LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) as a means to make black-box machine-learning models understandable. It links the risk of untrustworthy, opaque predictions to a concrete implementation—training a sparse linear surrogate around each prediction—and validates the approach through simulated and human-subject experiments that demonstrate improved trust and better model selection.  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[90]  
The chain of reasoning from risk to interventions is short and explicitly stated in the abstract, allowing clear node and edge construction. The main uncertainty lies in inferring life-cycle staging for the two interventions, which is not explicitly labeled in the abstract.  

Inference strategy justification  
Only moderate inference was needed to (1) separate the abstract’s single framework (LIME) into component concept nodes and (2) articulate two concrete interventions—deploying explanations to end-users and using explanations during pre-deployment auditing—both clearly implied by the authors’ stated use cases.  

Extraction completeness explanation  
All distinct reasoning elements appearing in the abstract (risk, lack of interpretability, local surrogate insight, design approach, algorithmic mechanism, experimental validation, and two deployment-relevant uses) are represented. No additional concepts were left unconnected.  

Key limitations  
1. The abstract does not provide quantitative metrics, so evidence strength is estimated qualitatively.  
2. Detailed algorithmic variants (e.g., submodular pick) are not fully captured because of limited space.  
3. Interventions derived from broader LIME literature may add detail not present here and would require separate sources.
